sentences: This is The Arnolfini Portrait by Jan van Eyck.
On an oak panel just over 82 centimetres tall, a couple stands side by side in their room, hand in hand.
It is a small picture, but it rewards very close looking.
The man is probably Giovanni Arnolfini, an Italian merchant who worked in Bruges.
Exactly which Giovanni of the family he is, and who his wife was, is still debated.
He raises his right hand, as if taking an oath.
Look up at the brass chandelier.
Of its six holders, only one, at the front left, holds a lit candle.
A single flame burning in broad daylight has invited many different interpretations, and none is certain.
On the wall below it, an elegant Latin signature reads Jan van Eyck was here, 1434.
Written as if directly on the wall, it hints that the painter was a witness to this scene, not just its maker.
The mirror's frame holds tiny roundels, each about half a fingernail wide, painted with scenes of Christ's Passion.
His death and resurrection are on the wife's side, and scenes from his life are on the husband's.
Look into the convex mirror and you see the couple from behind, plus two figures entering through the doorway: exactly where we are standing.
Many believe one of them is van Eyck himself.
To the right of the mirror, a small brush hangs from the bedpost, topped by a carved saint.
She is most often identified as Saint Margaret, patron saint of childbirth, while the brush is thought to stand for household duties.
The woman is not pregnant.
Her full silhouette comes from gathering up her heavy green skirts, as fashion then required.
We see exactly the same look in paintings of virgin saints from the period.
The shaggy little dog at their feet is often read as a symbol of loyalty.
In the lower left lie the wooden overshoes the man has taken off, and further back on the floor stands a pair of red shoes.
The oranges on the windowsill and the chest were a sign of wealth in the Netherlands at the time.
Soft daylight from the window quietly picks out every object in the room, from fur to brass to wood.
Van Eyck built all of this out of thin, glowing layers of oil glaze, laid one over another.
After passing through many owners, the painting was bought by the National Gallery in London in 1842.
Step back and think of those two figures in the mirror's doorway.
Inside the mirror, we are the guests who have just walked into this room.
What have we come here to witness?
